tapeLine: The 10-year cleared its own 2023 high to touch 5.02% Tuesday, the highest since 2007, as Fed funds futures priced Wednesday's hike at roughly 94.5%, up from 87.3% a day earlier. Oil held near six-week highs after the Associated Press and Reuters both reported the Saudi pipeline could take three to six weeks to repair — not the “soon” the U.S. energy secretary suggested Monday. Stocks fell Monday on the AI-slowdown story before President Trump and China’s foreign ministry both rejected it outright, and futures point lower again this morning. New York’s Empire State index swung negative for the first time since June, and Sequence Holdings and Michael Dell’s family office agreed to take insurance broker Baldwin Group private for $7.7bn — a deal that is mostly equity and assumed debt, not fresh leverage, so the financing test this brief has run since 10 September stays open one day out from the vote.
matters:
Fed funds futures now put the odds of a quarter-point hike at Wednesday's meeting at 94.5%, up from 87.3% a day earlier, according to CME FedWatch data cited by Bloomberg — effectively a lock heading into the 14:00 ET decision and Chair Warsh's 14:30 press conference. It would be the Fed's first hike since July 2023. The blackout that began 5 September holds through the vote, so no official has been able to respond to any of the last 24 hours of news.

The bond market moved first and furthest: the 10-year Treasury yield rose to 5.02% Tuesday, clearing its own October 2023 cycle high to reach the highest level since 2007. Oil is doing part of that work — Brent was near $106.93 and WTI near $102.65 Tuesday morning — and the supply shock behind it got longer, not shorter, overnight. Monday's brief ran the U.S. energy secretary's comment that the Saudi pipeline should reopen “soon”; by that same afternoon, sources told the Associated Press repairs could take three to five weeks and told Reuters five to six weeks, with one independent analyst telling reporters the damage shown in satellite images could take months to fully fix. “Soon” was the optimistic end of a range, not a timeline.

The AI-slowdown story kept moving too, but sideways into politics rather than toward the Fed. President Trump dismissed the industry's own calls for a pause, blaming a “SICK conspiracy” for the voter backlash on AI data centers and arguing “whoever wins AI, wins” against China. Beijing responded in kind: foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun called the warnings from Amodei, Altman and Musk “fear-mongering” that would “disrupt the process of global AI governance.” U.S. equities fell Monday on the original story — the Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq all closed lower — and futures point lower again this morning, but the disagreement is now between governments, not between the industry and its regulators.

New York's Empire State manufacturing index swung negative for the first time since June, falling to -8.7 from 11.9 in August, a real domestic data point landing the same morning as the yield milestone. On the financing thread this brief has tracked since 10 September, the closest thing yet to a sponsor-financed LBO printed Monday: Sequence Holdings and Michael Dell's DFO Management agreed to take The Baldwin Group private for $7.7bn, but roughly $4.6bn of that is equity and the debt in the deal is existing Baldwin debt being assumed or refinanced, not freshly raised acquisition leverage. Grab's same-day, all-cash purchase of a majority stake in Atome Financial for $1.49bn is a cleaner data point for the pattern: cash is still funding deals, one day out from the vote.

Invalidation: a Wednesday surprise — a smaller hike, a split vote, or dovish language in the Summary of Economic Projections — would matter more than usual given how one-sided positioning already is; anything short of the fully-priced 25bp move risks an outsized reaction precisely because so little probability is left on the other side.

deals.what: Sequence Holdings and Michael Dell's family office (DFO Management) agree to take The Baldwin Group private for $7.7bn
deals.number: Announced 14 Sep: Baldwin shareholders get $32.50 per share in cash, an 88% premium to the 17 June unaffected price. The deal comprises roughly $4.6bn of equity purchase price plus about $3.1bn of net debt assumed or refinanced; Sequence (a VC-backed, permanent-capital holding company) and DFO are the buyers, with Baldwin employees retaining a minority stake. Expected to close Q1 2027.
deals.readthrough: The closest thing to a sponsor buyout since this brief started counting on 10 September, and it still isn't a clean match: the debt in the deal is existing Baldwin debt being assumed or refinanced, not new acquisition leverage raised to fund the purchase, and the buyers are a permanent-capital vehicle and a family office rather than a classic PE fund. The test — a large, freshly debt-financed sponsor LBO printing before the Fed votes — is still open with one trading day left.

deals.what: Grab Holdings agrees to buy 60% of BNPL platform Atome Financial for $1.49bn in cash
deals.number: Announced 15 Sep via 6-K filing: Grab will pay $1.49bn in cash for a controlling 60% stake in Atome Financial, including $0.26bn of primary growth capital as Phase 1, funded entirely from Grab's existing cash. The remaining 40% is pre-agreed to transfer roughly two years after close under a valuation formula rather than a fixed price. Expected to complete by Q3 2027.
deals.readthrough: A cleaner data point for the pattern than Baldwin: another acquirer paying with its own balance sheet, not a lender's, in the same week the 10-year cleared 5% for the first time since 2007. The cash-over-debt read this brief has tracked since 10 September holds again.

regime.tag: record long yield, hike near-lock, pipeline shock getting longer
regime.sizing: The 10-year has cleared its own 2023 high to the highest level since 2007 and the hike is priced above 94%, so Wednesday's SEP and Warsh's press conference, not the vote itself, are the remaining swing factors. The pipeline's now-reported three-to-six-week repair window pushes the oil shock's duration further out than Monday's 'reopen soon' framing implied.

secondOrder: Three threads from Monday are still running, and each moved a specific, falsifiable amount today rather than just continuing. The Fed thread firmed: CME FedWatch's odds went from roughly 86–90% Friday to 94.5% by Tuesday morning, per Bloomberg, and the 10-year didn't just approach the 2023 high, it cleared it, printing the first sub-2007 yield level in almost two decades. The AI thread got more political, not less: a sitting U.S. president and a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson are now the ones arguing with Amodei, Altman and Musk, which is a different, more durable story than three tech CEOs agreeing with each other. And the oil thread got longer, not shorter: Monday's brief ran the U.S. energy secretary's 'soon,' and by that same afternoon the AP and Reuters were both reporting repair estimates measured in weeks, which means Wednesday's Fed decision arrives with the supply shock's timeline actually worse than it looked 24 hours earlier, not resolved. None of that changes the financing test this brief has run since 10 September: Tuesday's closest candidate, the Baldwin Group take-private, is majority equity with assumed debt, not fresh leverage, so cash is still the pattern and nothing forces that to change before tomorrow's 2pm vote.

scorecard.text: The 14 September brief argued the AI-slowdown story was “a standalone equity story, not a rates one” with “nothing to do with the Fed.” That held: the story moved further from monetary policy, not closer, when President Trump called it a “SICK conspiracy” on 13–14 September and said “whoever wins AI, wins,” and China's foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun separately dismissed the CEOs' warnings as “fear-mongering” that would “disrupt the process of global AI governance.” Two governments, not central bankers, are now the story's counterparties.

The same brief's overnight section ran the U.S. energy secretary's Monday comment that the Saudi pipeline should reopen “soon,” with no independent repair estimate attached. Reporting already circulating that same day undercut it: sources told the Associated Press repairs could take three to five weeks and told Reuters five to six weeks, with one independent analyst suggesting the damage shown in satellite images could take months to fully fix. “Soon” was the more optimistic of two competing estimates, and the brief ran only the optimistic one.

The test set on 10 September — whether a large, freshly debt-financed sponsor buyout prints before the Fed votes — still hasn't been cleanly met or missed. Sequence Holdings and Michael Dell's DFO Management agreed on 14 September to take The Baldwin Group private for $7.7bn, the closest candidate yet, but roughly $4.6bn of that is equity and the debt is existing Baldwin debt being assumed or refinanced rather than new acquisition leverage. One trading day remains before Wednesday's decision.
